title: Acute stroke care: thrombolysis, thrombectomy and the first 24 hours
blurb: Know the treatment windows, the blood pressure, glucose and oxygen targets, and the nursing care that protects the brain in the first day.
question: Mrs Achterberg, 74, has a CT scan that excludes haemorrhage 2 hours after her right arm became weak. Her blood pressure is 198/112 mmHg and she is being considered for thrombolysis. What blood pressure should the team aim for before treatment?

teach.body: An acute ischaemic stroke is a blocked artery starving part of the brain; an intracerebral haemorrhage is a bleed. They look the same at the bedside, so the first job is urgent brain imaging. Once a bleed is excluded, clot-busting (thrombolysis) and clot retrieval (thrombectomy) can restore blood flow, but only within set time windows. Plain English: every minute counts, and the clock starts when the person was last known to be well.

teach.h: From the front door to the stroke unit

steps.label: Image now
steps.sub: Non-enhanced CT if thrombolysis or thrombectomy possible

steps.label: Reperfuse
steps.sub: Thrombolysis within 4.5 h; thrombectomy if eligible

steps.label: Stroke unit
steps.sub: Swallow screen, aspirin, positioning, early mobilising

teach.caption: Ask for the time the person was last known to be well, not the time they were found.

head: Treatment
Window
Condition
teach.caption: Wake-up strokes are timed from when the person was last known to be well, so some may still reach thrombectomy.

teach.h: Four numbers for the first day

items.label: BP to reach or go below before thrombolysis
SpO2 at which supplemental oxygen is given
no high-intensity mobilisation for those needing help

teach.h: Protect the penumbra: BP, glucose, oxygen
teach.body: Around the core of dead tissue is brain that can still be saved. Keep it supplied. Consider lowering BP to 185/110 or below in thrombolysis candidates. Otherwise, NICE advises antihypertensive treatment in acute ischaemic stroke only in a hypertensive emergency (such as encephalopathy, aortic dissection or heart failure). Keep glucose between 4 and 11 mmol/L. Give oxygen only if saturation falls below 95%; routine oxygen does not help.

rows.label: BP limit
values: Drop no more than 60 in 1 h

teach.caption: ICH rapid lowering applies within 6 hours with systolic 150–220 mmHg, unless excluded (for example GCS below 6 or early surgery).

teach.text: Aspirin timing differs. In suspected TIA, give aspirin 300 mg immediately. In acute stroke, aspirin 300 mg waits until brain imaging has excluded haemorrhage, then is given within 24 hours and daily for 2 weeks. If the swallow screen is failed, give it rectally or by enteral tube, not by mouth.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Okafor on the hyperacute unit
teach.body: Mr Okafor, 68, was last seen well at 07:30 and arrives at 09:10 with facial droop and dysphasia. CT excludes bleeding. His BP is 192/108, glucose 6.4 and SpO2 97% on air. The nurse flags that BP must be at or below 185/110 for thrombolysis, gives no oxygen, keeps him nil by mouth until a swallow screen, and records neurological observations. CT angiography shows a proximal occlusion, so he is referred for thrombectomy too.

teach.caption: NICE NG128 rec 1.5.1. The BTS guideline also warns that unnecessary oxygen may harm non-hypoxaemic people with stroke.

teach.h: Nursing care in the first 24 hours
items: Swallow screen by a trained professional before any oral food, fluid or medicine.
Assess each person's needs and preferences for head position.
Help them sit out, stand or walk as soon as their condition permits; no high-intensity mobilisation in the first 24 hours if they need help.
VTE: do not use anti-embolism stockings; consider intermittent pneumatic compression within 3 days if immobile.
Keep glucose 4–11 mmol/L and escalate deterioration promptly.
Thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) within 4.5 hours once haemorrhage is excluded.
Thrombectomy within 6 hours, or up to 24 hours from last known well if brain is salvageable.
BP 185/110 or lower before thrombolysis; glucose 4–11; oxygen if SpO2 below 95%.
Aspirin 300 mg within 24 hours after imaging, rectal or enteral if dysphagic, for 2 weeks.
No stockings in acute stroke: consider IPC. No high-intensity mobilising in the first 24 hours.

summary: You can now apply the thrombolysis and thrombectomy windows from the time last known well, and keep BP, glucose and oxygen within NICE targets. You can also give aspirin safely by the right route and plan positioning, mobilisation and VTE prevention for the first 24 hours.

A.q: Mr Haddad, 66, has acute ischaemic stroke confirmed on CT and is a candidate for intravenous thrombolysis. His blood pressure is 194/106 mmHg. To what level should blood pressure reduction be considered before treatment?
options: 160/90 mmHg or lower
140/90 mmHg or lower
185/110 mmHg or lower
220/120 mmHg or lower
A.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.5.10: consider reducing BP to 185/110 mmHg or lower in people who are candidates for intravenous thrombolysis.

whyNot.0: 160/90 is not a stroke threshold; lowering this far is not what NG128 recommends before thrombolysis.
whyNot.1: 140/90 is the clinic hypertension diagnosis threshold in NG136, not the pre-thrombolysis target.
whyNot.3: 220/120 is too high; thrombolysis candidates need BP at or below 185/110.

A.q: Mrs Lindqvist, 80, is admitted to the stroke unit with an ischaemic stroke. She is alert, her respiratory rate is 16 and her oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. What is the most appropriate action regarding oxygen?
options: Give no supplemental oxygen and keep monitoring
Nasal cannulae at 2 L/min aiming for 98%
Reservoir mask at 15 L/min for 24 hours
28% Venturi mask pending a blood gas
A.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.5.1: give supplemental oxygen to people with stroke only if their saturation drops below 95%. Routine oxygen is not recommended.

whyNot.1: Her saturation is above 95%, so oxygen is not indicated; pushing her to 98% gives no benefit.
whyNot.2: A reservoir mask is for critical illness; she is not hypoxaemic.
whyNot.3: A Venturi mask is for people at risk of hypercapnia who need oxygen; she does not need oxygen at all.

A.q: A nurse is reviewing the capillary glucose of a man admitted 6 hours ago with an acute stroke. Within which range should blood glucose be maintained?
options: 6–10 mmol/L
4–7 mmol/L
7–14 mmol/L
4–11 mmol/L
A.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.5.2: maintain blood glucose between 4 and 11 mmol/L in people with acute stroke.

whyNot.0: 6–10 mmol/L is the JBDS perioperative target for people with diabetes having surgery.
whyNot.1: 4–7 mmol/L is the NG17 pre-meal target for type 1 diabetes self-monitoring.
whyNot.2: 7–14 mmol/L would allow harmful hyperglycaemia and is not a stroke target.

B.q: Mr Bello's CT excludes haemorrhage. His symptoms began 3 hours 50 minutes ago. Which statement about intravenous thrombolysis is correct?
options: He is past the 3-hour limit for thrombolysis
He is inside the 4.5-hour window from onset
He has 12 hours, as for primary PCI
He must first be scored with ABCD2
B.why: NICE NG128 and TA990: alteplase or tenecteplase can be given within 4.5 hours of symptom onset once intracranial haemorrhage is excluded.

whyNot.0: The window for both alteplase and tenecteplase is 4.5 hours, not 3 hours.
whyNot.2: 12 hours is the STEMI primary PCI window in NG185, not a stroke thrombolysis window.
whyNot.3: ABCD2 is not used; NG128 removed risk scoring even for TIA.

B.q: Mrs Dube went to bed well at 23:00 and her husband found her with left-sided weakness at 06:30. When the team decides whether she can still have thrombectomy, which time is used?
options: 06:30, when her husband found her
Her arrival time in the emergency department
23:00, when she was last known to be well
The time her first CT scan was reported
B.why: NICE NG128 recs 1.4.6–1.4.7 time thrombectomy from when the person was last known to be well, including wake-up strokes (up to 24 hours if brain tissue is salvageable).

whyNot.0: Being found with symptoms is not the onset; the stroke may have started any time after 23:00.
whyNot.1: Arrival time understates how long the brain has been ischaemic.
whyNot.3: The scan report time has no bearing on when the stroke began.

B.q: Mr Patel has an ischaemic stroke, haemorrhage has been excluded, and he has failed his swallow screen. How should his antiplatelet treatment be given today?
options: 75 mg aspirin dispersed in water by mouth
Aspirin 300 mg rectally or by enteral tube
Withhold aspirin until a specialist SLT review
300 mg aspirin orally with thickened fluid
B.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.4.9: aspirin 300 mg within 24 hours, rectally or by enteral tube if the person has dysphagia, then daily for 2 weeks.

whyNot.0: Nothing can go by mouth after a failed screen, and the acute dose is 300 mg, not 75 mg.
whyNot.2: Aspirin should not wait for SLT review; it is due within 24 hours by a non-oral route.
whyNot.3: A failed screen means no oral medicine until assessed, whatever the fluid consistency.

C.q: Mrs Osei, 79, had an ischaemic stroke 10 hours ago. She needs two staff to stand and is keen to get up. Her observations are stable. Which mobilisation plan follows NICE guidance?
options: Strict bed rest for 48 hours before sitting out
High-intensity walking practice this afternoon
Wait until she can stand without help to sit out
Help her sit out as able; no high-intensity work yet
C.why: NICE NG128 recs 1.7.2–1.7.3: help people sit out, stand or walk as soon as their condition permits, but do not offer high-intensity mobilisation in the first 24 hours to those who need help.

whyNot.0: Routine bed rest is not recommended; she should be helped up when her condition permits.
whyNot.1: She needs help to stand, so high-intensity mobilisation in the first 24 hours is not offered.
whyNot.2: Waiting for independent standing delays rehabilitation; NG128 supports assisted early sitting out.

C.q: Mr Novak is immobile 2 days after an acute stroke. The healthcare assistant asks whether to fit anti-embolism stockings. Which response is best?
options: Measure and fit thigh-length stockings now
Fit below-knee stockings at night
Stockings are not used; IPC may be considered
Fit stockings once he is first mobilising
C.why: NICE NG89 recs 1.4.2–1.4.3: do not offer anti-embolism stockings for VTE prophylaxis in acute stroke; consider intermittent pneumatic compression, started within 3 days, if the person is immobile.

whyNot.0: Anti-embolism stockings are not offered after acute stroke, whatever their length.
whyNot.1: Below-knee stockings are still anti-embolism stockings and are not recommended in acute stroke.
whyNot.3: Stockings are not part of stroke VTE prevention at any stage of mobilising.

C.q: Ms Chen, 58, arrives 4 hours after onset. CT shows an intracerebral haemorrhage, GCS 14, systolic BP 196 mmHg. Rapid blood pressure lowering is started. What target should the nurse expect?
options: Systolic 140 or lower, falling no more than 60 in 1 hour
185/110 or lower, the pre-thrombolysis threshold
Systolic 120 within 30 minutes of starting
Systolic 160, with no limit on the speed of fall
C.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.5.6: in acute ICH, aim for systolic 140 mmHg or lower while making sure the drop does not exceed 60 mmHg within 1 hour of starting treatment.

whyNot.1: 185/110 applies to ischaemic stroke before thrombolysis, which is never given for haemorrhage.
whyNot.2: A fall from 196 to 120 within 30 minutes exceeds the 60 mmHg-in-1-hour limit.
whyNot.3: 160 is above the target and NG128 sets a limit on how quickly BP may fall.

reteach.title: Two clocks and three dials
reteach.question: Picture two clocks and three dials on the wall of the hyperacute unit. What do they show?

blocks.body: Clock one: thrombolysis, which stops at 4.5 hours from onset. Clock two: thrombectomy, which runs to 6 hours and, for selected people with salvageable brain, up to 24 hours from last known well. The three dials are blood pressure (185/110 or lower if thrombolysing), glucose (4–11 mmol/L) and oxygen (on only if SpO2 is below 95%). Nothing starts until a scan has excluded a bleed.

items.label: Last known well: the clock starts
Selected thrombectomy; aspirin 300 mg given by now

blocks.text: Found at 06:30 does not mean onset at 06:30. If someone woke with symptoms, the clock started when they were last known to be well.

explain.body: Alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of onset once haemorrhage is excluded. Thrombectomy within 6 hours for a confirmed proximal anterior occlusion, and up to 24 hours from last known well if imaging shows brain that can be saved.

test.q: Which treatment may be offered to a selected person last known to be well 14 hours ago with a proximal anterior circulation occlusion and salvageable brain on imaging?
options: Intravenous alteplase
Mechanical thrombectomy
Intravenous tenecteplase
Aspirin 300 mg before CT
test.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.4.6: thrombectomy for people last known well 6–24 hours previously with a proximal anterior occlusion and potential to salvage brain tissue.

whyNot.0: Alteplase is limited to 4.5 hours from onset.
whyNot.3: Aspirin is given after imaging has excluded a bleed, not before.

explain.body: Before thrombolysis, consider lowering BP to 185/110 or below. Otherwise, in acute ischaemic stroke, treat BP only in a hypertensive emergency. In intracerebral haemorrhage within 6 hours with systolic 150–220, aim for 140 or lower without dropping more than 60 mmHg in an hour.

test.q: Mrs Ruiz has an ischaemic stroke, is outside the thrombolysis window and has a BP of 178/98 with no other concerns. What does NICE advise about antihypertensive treatment now?
options: Start oral amlodipine to reach 140/90
Lower it to 185/110 using IV labetalol
Reserve it for a hypertensive emergency
Aim for systolic 140 within 1 hour
test.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.5.9: antihypertensive treatment in acute ischaemic stroke is recommended in a hypertensive emergency with serious concomitant problems such as encephalopathy or aortic dissection.

whyNot.0: Routine BP lowering to 140/90 is not recommended in the acute phase.
whyNot.1: Her BP is already below 185/110 and she is not a thrombolysis candidate.
whyNot.3: Rapid lowering to 140 is the ICH plan, not for ischaemic stroke.

explain.body: Keep blood glucose 4–11 mmol/L. Give supplemental oxygen when SpO2 falls below 95%; routine oxygen is not recommended for people who are not hypoxaemic.

test.q: A man 8 hours after an ischaemic stroke has SpO2 93% on air. What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat the reading in 4 hours
Start oxygen and escalate
Record it and keep him on air
Sit him upright and recheck tomorrow
test.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.5.1: give supplemental oxygen if saturation drops below 95%. A new low reading also needs escalation to find the cause.

whyNot.0: Waiting 4 hours leaves him hypoxaemic below the NG128 threshold.
whyNot.2: 93% is below 95%, so oxygen is indicated.
whyNot.3: Positioning may help but he still needs oxygen now and review.

explain.body: Aspirin 300 mg within 24 hours once a bleed is excluded (rectal or enteral if dysphagic), daily for 2 weeks. Sit out when able, no high-intensity mobilising in the first 24 hours for those needing help. No anti-embolism stockings; consider IPC within 3 days if immobile.

test.q: For how long is aspirin 300 mg daily continued after an acute ischaemic stroke before definitive long-term antithrombotic treatment starts?
options: 2 weeks
3 months
7 days
48 hours
test.why: NICE NG128 rec 1.4.9: continue aspirin 300 mg daily until 2 weeks after onset, then start long-term antithrombotic treatment (earlier if discharged before then).

whyNot.1: 3 months is the minimum anticoagulation period for VTE (NG158), not the aspirin course.
whyNot.2: 7 days is the minimum LMWH course for medical VTE prophylaxis (NG89).
whyNot.3: 48 hours is far shorter than the NG128 course.
